conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. To do that, I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screening that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past seven days. It isn’t a test of your parenting—just a way to see how you’re coping so we can offer the right support. Everything you share stays confidential, and you can pause or stop at any time. Ready to begin?

Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

As much as I want to laugh like I used to… it just doesn’t come easily anymore. Sometimes my partner will make a joke or I’ll see something silly on my phone and I almost feel like I should be laughing, but it just sort of fizzles out. I’d say I’ve managed a genuine laugh maybe once or twice this week, and even then it felt forced. Mostly I’m too tired or worried about the baby to find anything very funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not very often… I’d say only once or twice, and even those laughs felt kind of half-hearted. Most of the time I’m too worn out or on-edge about the baby to find much funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, not much. I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet hour to read. Now it feels like there’s nothing to look forward to. I’ll think, “Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel like myself,” but when tomorrow comes I’m still just going through the motions. I did force myself to meet a friend for a quick stroller walk on Tuesday, and for a minute I thought it might feel good, but the enjoyment lasted maybe five minutes before I was worrying again.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… way too often. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right or I missed his sleepy cues.” Yesterday he wouldn’t nap and I sat there crying, convinced it was because I’m a terrible mom. Even little stuff, like spilling a little pumped milk, feels like proof I’m failing. I know, logically, babies cry and accidents happen, but I still hear this voice saying I should be better at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there with the baby asleep in the bassinet, and suddenly my heart starts racing—like something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s wrong. I check if he’s breathing every few minutes, and if he stirs I jump up convinced he’s choking or in pain. Sometimes the worry just sits in my chest all day, like a heavy knot, and I can’t point to any real reason for it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… a few times this week. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts pounding, I feel shaky, and I have to remind myself to breathe. One night I was rocking the baby in the dark and out of nowhere I was sure something terrible was about to happen to him. I couldn’t tell you what, just this overwhelming dread. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me feeling drained and on-edge the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. I start the day thinking, “I only need to feed him, change him, maybe fold that laundry,” and suddenly the pile feels like a mountain. If he cries for more than a few minutes, I’m sure I’m failing. I keep telling myself other moms handle this, but I still end up in tears because I can’t keep up. I’m managing the basics—he’s fed, diapered, safe—but it feels like I’m barely treading water and the smallest extra task makes me feel like I’m drowning.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening most nights. I’ll finally get the baby down, crawl into bed exhausted, and then my mind just starts spinning— replaying everything I think I did wrong, worrying about what might go wrong tomorrow. Some nights I drift off okay but jerk awake an hour later with my heart racing. I’d say four, maybe five nights out of the past week I’ve lain there for an hour or more before I can fall back asleep, even when the baby’s still quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. It’s like this gray cloud that just hangs there. I’ll be feeding the baby and suddenly feel tears coming for no real reason. I wouldn’t say every single moment—I’ll have a short spell here or there where I feel kind of “okay”—but the sadness always creeps back in. It’s not the dramatic sobbing every day; more like a steady ache that makes everything feel heavy and colorless.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened several times this week. Not all-day sobbing, but I’ll be rocking the baby or looking at him sleeping and suddenly my eyes just well up. I cried in the shower yesterday because the thought “I should be enjoying this” hit me and I realized I wasn’t. I’d say four or five days out of the last seven there’ve been tears—sometimes just a quick burst, sometimes longer if I’m feeling really overwhelmed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. I’m exhausted and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can take care of my baby.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a constant gray heaviness-laughs come rarely and feel forced, things you once anticipated now seem colorless, and most days carry a steady ache of sadness. You described checking your sleeping baby's breathing over and over, heart racing with nameless dread, and blaming yourself for every cry or spilled drop of milk. Even simple tasks feel like mountains, and nights bring restless replaying of worries instead of rest. Yet through it all you remain devoted to your baby's safety and simply wish to feel better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only 1–2 half-hearted laughs in 7 days, clearly less than usual, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports absence of anticipatory pleasure and only fleeting enjoyment, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "way too often" and gives multiple specific examples of intense self-blame, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intense, unexplained anxiety with physical symptoms and constant vigilance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple discrete panic-like episodes this week with physical and cognitive symptoms, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent overwhelm and tears yet still managing basics, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports difficulty sleeping on 4–5 nights in the past week, lying awake for over an hour due to racing thoughts, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sadness on "most days," spontaneous tears, pervasive "gray cloud" and "heavy and colorless" mood, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes 4–5 of the past 7 days, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 23 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the threshold indicating probable major depression with peripartum onset. You endorse core symptoms such as marked loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), persistent low or depressed mood most days, frequent crying, disproportionate self-blame, and recurrent anxiety or panic without clear triggers. Sleep disruption, fatigue, and feeling unable to cope add further evidence. Per <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, five or more depressive symptoms present most days for two weeks can support the diagnosis. You report no self-harm thoughts, so immediate safety concerns are lower, but functional impairment is evident and warrants prompt clinical evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to discuss these results and consider therapy and/or medication options
2. Ask your provider about evidence-based treatments such as <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med>, both effective for postpartum depression
3. Enlist trusted family or friends to help with household tasks, night feeds, or baby care so you can rest; even short breaks can reduce overwhelm
4. Practice gentle daily self-check-ins: name one thing you did well today (e.g., fed the baby, took a shower) to counter harsh self-criticism
5. Keep a simple sleep routine-dim lights, no screens during night feeds, brief relaxation breathing-to improve <sym>insomnia</sym>
6. Stay connected: schedule low-pressure social contacts such as a 10-minute phone call or a walk with another parent; isolation can intensify low mood
7. Monitor mood daily; if thoughts of self-harm develop, seek emergency help immediately or call your local crisis line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – 10-item EPDS responses reviewed.

<sym>Endorsed symptoms</sym>: marked anhedonia, persistent low mood, daily tearfulness, excessive self-blame/guilt, intrusive worries, panic-like episodes, feeling overwhelmed, initial and middle insomnia, diminished enjoyment with infant.

Pattern: symptoms present ≥5/7 days per week, causing subjective impairment but no self-harm ideation.

Risk flags: moderate–high for postpartum depression and comorbid anxiety; notable maternal distress and functional impairment; no safety concerns voiced.

Screening observation: findings exceed threshold for routine follow-up; recommend formal clinical evaluation for PPD / PPA and psychosocial support.
